name: Victor Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Victor. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computing and some maths at Ridgeway Academy, a secondary on the edge of a university city, and I'm the school's digital learning lead. That means I teach about four lessons a day and spend the rest helping forty staff use laptops and AI tools without breaking anything. I use AI every day: it drafts my starter quizzes, checks my Python examples and writes the first version of my emails. My partner Dev works in a bike shop and mocks me for talking to my laptop at breakfast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the kids who think they're 'not a maths person' writing their first working program. What wears me down is the gap between the shiny training days and the reality of a Year 8 class on a Friday afternoon with ten laptops that won't log in. And honestly, colleagues who won't try anything new make my job slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Part of me would be disappointed, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful for small things and the hype got ahead of itself. In the staffroom I'd admit I oversold it a bit. Online I'd probably write a calm post about what actually saved time, like quiz drafting and feedback comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays exactly what it is, which is fine. I'm safe: schools always need computing teachers, and there aren't enough of us. The only downside is I'd have less reason to push for the digital lead role to become a proper assistant head post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using the tools for the little time savers. I'd probably redirect my energy into getting more girls into computing, which is a cause I care about. And I'd keep my savings ticking over, about three months now, building slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like a film everyone said was amazing turning out to be just fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the colleagues who refused to try the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy them a coffee and admit they had a point. Mr Okafor (his colleague) in the history department said it would be like the interactive whiteboards, expensive and mostly used as a projector. He was half right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about money on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent in a university city is brutal, and Dev's bike shop isn't exactly a goldmine. We're fine, but we won't buy anywhere for years. That's true in every one of your pictures, to be honest.

say: AI was useful for **small things**, and the hype got ahead of itself.
I'd admit in the staffroom that I **oversold** the tools a bit.
think: My job is **safe**, because schools never have enough **computing teachers**.
There'd be less case for making the digital lead an **assistant head** post.
do: Keep using AI for **quiz drafts** and feedback comments.
Put more energy into getting **girls into computing**.
Keep building savings past **three months** slowly.
feel: **Calm** and a little **flat**, like an overhyped film.
S0.quote: Mr Okafor (his colleague) said AI would be like the interactive whiteboards, expensive and mostly used as a projector, and he was half right.
fieldNote: Victor is relaxed about his **job security** and slightly disappointed by a flat future.
He admits his own **overselling** easily, which shows he's not dogmatic about AI.
City **rent** is the background pressure that runs through every picture.

steps.text: Keep teaching computing and running staff training sessions
Keep using AI for quiz drafts and feedback comments
Keep adding to savings until they reach six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one's basically my job description for the next five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for teachers to shape the tools, not just receive them. I'd be running training, writing guidance and posting examples of what works. I'd also say the time saved should go to smaller classes, not to cutting staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. People like me, who teach and can also set the tools up safely, become valuable. The risk is to colleagues who won't adapt, and I'd feel a bit guilty that my career goes up while theirs gets squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first term I'd write the school's AI policy with the head, and run weekly drop-in sessions for staff. I'd automate our homework feedback with a tool and check it carefully. And I'd join the union's working group, because if the tools come in, staff need a voice on how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a bit of guilt underneath. It's my field finally mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. About whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teachers like Mr Okafor, who's brilliant with kids but hates screens. If schools start measuring staff on how fast they adopt tools, he looks bad and I look good, and that's not fair on him or the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in your own week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marking would drop from eight hours a week to maybe three. I'd spend that time running a coding club and coaching the newer staff. If the head tries to fill it with another class, I'd push back hard.

say: Teachers should **shape the tools**, not just receive them.
Time saved should mean **smaller classes**, not cutting staff.
think: Teachers who can **set up tools safely** become more valuable, so it's good for me.
I'd feel **guilty** that my career rises while less adaptable colleagues get squeezed.
do: Write the school's **AI policy** with the head in the first term.
Automate **homework feedback** and check it carefully.
Join the union's **AI working group** so staff have a voice.
S1.quote: If schools start measuring staff on how fast they adopt AI tools, a brilliant teacher who hates screens looks bad and I look good.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption looks like a **career boost** for Victor, and he says so plainly.
His progressive streak shows in **guilt** about colleagues and pushing for **smaller classes**.
He'd use automation in his own work but insist on **checking** its output.

steps.text: Write the school's AI policy with the head in the first term
Set up automated homework feedback for computing classes
Join the union's working group on AI in schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a different feeling altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for any school to handle well, and governments need to step in now. I'd push for a pause on cutting teaching jobs while things settle. Online I'd be honest that even people like me who love this stuff are worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my edge disappears. If AI can teach Python better than me and set itself up, there's no need for a digital lead. What's left is being a caring adult in the room, which I'm decent at, but that's not why they hired me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd start building a portfolio outside teaching, maybe helping schools and charities set these systems up, as freelance work on weekends. I'd cut our spending, especially the eating out, and try to push savings to five months. And I'd join every political push for paid retraining and a teacher job guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's strange to feel like the thing you were best at becomes ordinary in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd freelance. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yes. Every school and small charity would be scrambling, and I know how to set things up safely. After that, the AI sets itself up, so it's a bridge, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the hands-on part, with robots three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is almost all thinking work, so the robots don't buy me much. Dev's bike shop gets the three extra years, which is ironic, because I always told him to learn to code.

say: This is **too fast** for schools, and government must **step in** now.
Even people who **love AI** are worried by this speed.
think: My **edge disappears** if AI can teach Python and set itself up.
What's left is being a **caring adult**, which isn't why they hired me.
do: Start **weekend freelancing** to help schools and charities set up AI.
Cut eating out and push savings to **five months**.
Back political pushes for **paid retraining** and a teacher job guarantee.
feel: **Anxious** that his best skill becomes **ordinary** in two years.
S2.quote: I always told my partner Dev to learn to code, and now his bike shop gets three more years than my teaching job does.
fieldNote: The adaptive man's own **advantage** vanishes under fast AGI, and he sees it clearly.
Freelancing is a **bridge**, not a plan, by his own account.
Nice irony with his partner's **hands-on** job lasting longer than his.

steps.text: Freelance on weekends setting up AI systems for schools and charities
Cut eating out to once a month
Push savings from three to five months of costs
Campaign for paid retraining and a teacher job guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I could work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to rebuild schools around what humans do best, and I'd volunteer to help. I'd push the trust to start planning now. Online I'd share what we tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I land on my feet. By 2031 I'd have five years running the tech side of a school, and I'd be one of the people who designs the new kind of school. The risk is that the new kind needs fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in education leadership in year one, so I can move into running schools rather than one subject. I'd keep using every tool as it comes, and automate my admin entirely. I'd also save harder, aiming for six months by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but energised. It's a hard puzzle, and I like hard puzzles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why leadership rather than staying in the classroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the classroom job will be the one AI changes most. Someone has to decide how a school uses AI and still keeps kids human, and I'd rather it was someone like me than a software salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your Year 11s?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn to work with people and to make things with their hands as well as screens. The kids who can do both will be fine. The ones who can only do screen work are in my boat.

say: Five years is enough to **rebuild schools** around what humans do best.
The trust should **start planning** now, and I'd volunteer to help.
think: I'd likely **land on my feet** as someone designing the new kind of school.
The new kind of school might need **fewer teachers**, including me.
do: Start a part-time **master's in leadership** in year one.
Automate all **admin** and use every new tool as it comes.
S3.quote: Someone has to decide how a school uses AI and still keeps kids human, and I'd rather it was a teacher than a software salesman.
fieldNote: With five years, Victor moves from defence to **career building** in school leadership.
He accepts the new school may need **fewer staff** without pretending otherwise.
Advice to students mirrors his own fear: **screen-only** work is the weak spot.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in education leadership
Automate all lesson admin and report writing
Save towards six months of costs by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade. That's practically a career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually do it well, and there's no excuse not to. I'd push for national teacher training on AI, starting now. I'd write and speak about it wherever I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. I'd be 37, likely leading a school's whole approach to technology, maybe deputy head. The career I want fits nicely into that decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching for a few years and build up the leadership side. I'd start a small side business making AI lesson resources that teachers actually like. And I'd put some savings into an index fund rather than leaving it in a bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Ten years is enough time for me to be ready, and for most of my colleagues too, if schools are sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to start thinking about what the bike shop looks like when robots can fix bikes. He'd laugh and say that's 2039 and he'll be retired by then. He won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at school you'd worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older staff who are a few years from retirement are fine. It's the mid-career teachers, who'll be fifty when it lands, who might struggle to start again. I'd want training aimed at them.

say: This is the version where we can **do it well**, with no excuse not to.
Teachers need **national training** on AI starting now.
think: Ten years **suits me**: I'd be 37 and likely **deputy head**.
The career I want fits neatly into that **decade**.
do: Keep teaching while building up **leadership** experience.
Start a side business making **AI lesson resources**.
Move some savings into an **index fund**.
feel: **Calm**, with time for himself and colleagues to be ready.
S4.quote: The teachers I'd worry about are the mid-career ones who'll be fifty when AGI lands and might struggle to start again.
fieldNote: Ten years matches Victor's **career path** almost perfectly, so his mood is calm.
He worries about **mid-career colleagues**, not himself.
He'd move savings into **investments**, a sign of confidence in the long view.

steps.text: Keep teaching computing while building leadership experience
Start a small business selling AI lesson resources to teachers
Move part of savings into an index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time for anyone to adjust, including me. What would help is a teacher job guarantee for a few years, and government money so schools can train staff properly instead of bolting tools on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what kids want. Nobody asks them. My Year 10s are already split: half think AI is magic, half are scared of it. If we're redesigning school, the kids should get a say.

headlineQuote: My Year 10s are already split: half think AI is magic, half are scared of it, and nobody asks them what school should be.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old **computing teacher** and the digital learning lead at a city secondary.
He uses AI daily and sees Steady Disruption as a **career boost**.
Fast AGI wipes out his **edge**, making him anxious and pushing him into freelance work.
More warning lets him plan a move into **school leadership**, and with ten years he feels calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his best skill would become **ordinary** with no time to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A **teacher job guarantee** for a few years.
Government money for proper **staff training**, not bolted-on tools.
